summary: This page discusses the practical bowl management system during the Yom Kippur blood service. Two gold stands in the Heichal hold the blood bowls sequentially - the HP never holds both bowls simultaneously, ensuring bull and goat blood are never confused. A Passover registration parallel illustrates the principle of systematic sequential handling in complex ritual situations. The Gemara also specifies the complete service order: bull inside the Holy of Holies, goat inside, then bull's Heichal service, then goat's Heichal service.

learning.ahaMoment: The stand system is not organizational convenience - it prevents the worst possible error on the holiest day. Physical arrangement serves spiritual integrity.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two bowls, two stands, one at a time: the system guarantees correct sequence even under pressure.
learning.learnerQuestion: How does the High Priest manage two blood bowls (bull and goat) during the Heichal services, given that both are needed sequentially?
learning.coreTension: The HP cannot hold both bowls simultaneously while sprinkling, but setting one down without a designated stand risks confusion or impurity; the practical management of two active blood containers requires a defined system.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud describes a stand in the Heichal where the HP places one bowl while working with the other; this stand enforces sequential handling and prevents the bowls from being confused or set on the floor.

takeaway.text: A designated stand in the Heichal allows the High Priest to place one blood bowl while working with the other; this system enforces proper sequential handling and prevents confusion between the bull and goat blood.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may not think about the practical logistics of managing two blood bowls simultaneously and may not realize the Talmud has a detailed, specified solution for this.

rashiTranslations.en: 'He does not hold that writing labels is a solution' - we do not rely on that, since sometimes he is not paying attention to examine
the writing. 'Because they get switched' - if he made two stands, he would set the goat's basin on one and
the bull's on the other, and when he comes to take the bull's blood, sometimes it gets switched on him
and he takes the goat's instead. Therefore, when there is only a single stand, he does not set this one down until he picks up
the other, and so the services come out in their proper order:
the goat's inside after the bull's, and the bull's
in the Heichal afterward, and only then the goat's.
'New shekels' - on the first shofar-box;
old shekels on the second; bird-offerings on the third;
young burnt-offering birds on the fourth; wood on
the fifth; frankincense on the sixth; gold
for the kapporet on the seventh; and six had
'voluntary offering' written on them. 'New shekels - these are the shekels of each and every year' -
one who owes this year's shekel and did not bring it
in Adar may bring it whenever he wishes,
and place it in the box for new shekels,
and the treasurers place them in the chamber
and from them they set aside the three collection-boxes before
Passover, before Shavuot, and before
Sukkot. 'He shall pay for the coming year' - and he places it
in the box for old shekels, and the treasurers add it
to the surplus of last year's chamber, from which they build
the city wall and its towers, as we learned in Shekalim
(chapter 4, mishnah 2). 'Bird-offerings - these are turtledoves' -
from the coins in that box, only
turtledoves are purchased. 'All of them are burnt-offerings' - R. Yehuda
follows his own reasoning, since he says there were no shofar-boxes for obligatory
bird-offerings. And regarding wood, frankincense, and gold for the kapporet,
it is explained in tractate Shekalim (chapter 6, mishnah 6):
one who donates wood puts money into that box, no
less than two logs' worth; and one who donates frankincense
brings money and places it into the frankincense box, and from it they purchase frankincense and burn it
as a voluntary offering on the outer altar. For gold for the kapporet, one who donates gold places money
into the box, and from it they purchase gold for sacred vessels, namely the basins called
'kaphorei zahav' in Ezra and Chronicles. 'And six for voluntary offerings' - for the altar's
'dessert' (supplementary offerings), to put into them money collected from all the shepherds, from the surplus of guilt-offerings
and sin-offerings, regarding which we learned that the animal shall graze until blemished, then be sold, and its proceeds fall to the voluntary-offering fund;
and in the last chapter of Menachot,
(107b): six shofar-boxes correspond to the six ancestral houses in every priestly watch, and each one recognizes his own day's box; and if the altar was idle on its day
because no one brought offerings, the members of that ancestral house would take their box's money
and purchase burnt-offerings with it, and that is the altar's 'dessert.' Learn from this, in any case,
that R. Yehuda does hold that writing labels works, since it is taught that they
had writing on them. 'A decree on account of a sin-offering whose owner died' -
lest one of the owners who placed money in the box has died,
and since there are sin-offerings among them, that money becomes the money of a sin-offering whose owner died,
which must go to the Dead Sea, and it would be found mixed with the valid coins and invalidate them,
and that is why it is because of the mixing. 'Whose owner has certainly died' - meaning we know of him that he died
after placing the money in the box but before an offering was brought. 'And let us set aside four zuz' -
the value of the sin-offering, and he means plain provincial zuz, of which there are eight to a Tyrian zuz, and that is the price of a single bird,
since we learned that bird-offerings once stood at a quarter-dinar each (Keritot 8a), and a quarter-dinar is
half a Tyrian dinar, which is four provincial zuz. 'He does not hold by the principle of retroactive designation' - we do not rely
on retroactive designation to permit something forbidden. 'One who buys wine from the Samaritans' - before they were decreed impure,
and he has no vessels into which to separate the terumah and tithes. 'They shall be terumah' - remaining inside it.
'And he waits' - this is the citation of the next teaching; the daf ends here, and the comment's own explanation is deferred to 56a.
